newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada sees growth without inflation.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada sees growth without inflation.

text.p: The Bank of Canada said on Friday that the growth of broad monetary aggregates points to strong economic growth in Canada, but without the risk of inflation in the near term.
The most narrow measure of money, M1, continues to grow rapidly, suggesting "that output will show robust growth throughout the first half of 1997," the central bank said in its Spring Review.

However, the bank's studies show that the rapid growth of M1 will not contribute to inflation and "is still consistent with inflation remaining within the Bank of Canada's inflation-control target range over the next two years," the report said.
Since M1 is still growing in response to lower interest rates, "rapid growth in M1 can continue for some time, as the adjustments of M1 to low interest rates is not yet complete," the bank said.

The bank also said that over the near term, rapid M1 growth is compatible with its inflation target range of one to three percent, but over the longer term, "it should be noted that the long-term trend rate of growth of M1 that is consistent with the inflation-control targets lies between three and five percent."
The bank estimates that M1 grew 11.1 percent in the first half of 1996 and 13.5 percent in the second half of 1996.
Market observerss say the rate of M1 growth in the first quarter of 1997 is widely considered to be about 22 percent.
In its Monetary Policy Report released on Thursday, the bank said it would keep a very close watch on the growth of M1.
The rapid growth in M1 can be linked to low interest rates, interest paid on current accounts, overal growth in non-personal deposits and growth in personal chequing accounts, the Spring Review said.
